entries.clue: Book is chilling about power and muscle (6)

indicators.note: ICES goes round the P, holding it inside

annotation.surface: A gripping thriller that also happens to build strength.
annotation.walkthrough: Read 'Book is chilling' as a review and you miss that 'is chilling' is a single verb, ICES, with power tucked inside it.
annotation.definitionFit: The biceps is the muscle at the front of the upper arm.

entries.clue: Runs into version of blues quite lacking it in American show (9)

indicators.note: R goes into the rearranged BLUES
a version of BLUES is its letters in a new order
QUITE lacking IT loses those two letters

annotation.surface: A singer drops the blues and rebrands for a racier American stage show.
annotation.walkthrough: Burlesque in the American sense is a variety show with striptease; 'it' is a sly nod to sex appeal, but here it is just two letters removed from QUITE.
annotation.definitionFit: American burlesque was a bawdy variety show of comedy and striptease.

entries.clue: Tricky clue, with pen filling space for working? (7)

indicators.note: a tricky CLUE is one twisted into a new order
BIC fills the rearranged letters

blocks.note: a Bic is a ballpoint pen brand

annotation.surface: A solver chews a pen over a hard clue, looking for room to work it out.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pictures scribbling in the margins, but 'space for working' is an office, not the white space round a grid.
annotation.definitionFit: A cubicle is a small partitioned workspace in an open-plan office.

entries.clue: Work up series 29 (5)

indicators.note: in a down clue, 'up' reads OP from bottom to top

annotation.walkthrough: 29 across is TEASER, and this puzzle's theme is its synonyms. OP is the standard short form of opus.
annotation.definitionFit: A poser is a puzzling question, a teaser.

entries.clue: Clearly friends will welcome Bishop before end of day (8)

indicators.note: the two PALs take B in between them
the end of DAY is its last letter

blocks.note: two pals, since friends is plural
B = bishop in chess notation, placed inside

annotation.surface: Friends plainly throw open the doors to a visiting bishop before nightfall.
annotation.walkthrough: The trick is that 'friends' is two PALs side by side, not PALS: the bishop sits between them.
annotation.definitionFit: Palpably means so plainly it can almost be touched, clearly.

entries.clue: Long story? End almost here, last bit to go, on reflection (6)

indicators.note: NEAR loses its final letter
a reflection shows everything backwards

blocks.note: what is almost here is near

annotation.surface: A weary listener hopes a long-winded tale is finally nearly over.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Almost' looks like the usual lop-off-a-letter signal, but 'almost here' is simply NEAR; 'last bit to go' does the cutting. The Aeneid is Virgil's Latin epic.
annotation.definitionFit: Virgil's Aeneid is an epic poem in twelve books, a long story indeed.

entries.clue: Iberia? Portugal and Spain almost all in sun, possibly (9)

indicators.note: ALL almost is ALL short of its last letter
a possible arrangement of the letters

blocks.note: P is Portugal's international car code

annotation.definitionNote: Iberia is one example of a peninsula, hence the question mark.
annotation.surface: A travel note about Iberia's two countries soaking up the sunshine.
annotation.walkthrough: Portugal and Spain look like part of the definition, but they are just their car codes. The question mark flags Iberia as one example of the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: The Iberian Peninsula holds Spain and Portugal, so Iberia is a peninsula.

entries.clue: French composer and American composer not finished with Australia (7)

indicators.note: BERLIN stops one letter short

blocks.note: Irving BERLIN without his last letter

annotation.surface: A concert pairing a French composer with an American one on an Australian tour.
annotation.walkthrough: Irving Berlin wrote 'White Christmas'; Hector Berlioz wrote the 'Symphonie fantastique'.
annotation.definitionFit: Hector Berlioz was a nineteenth-century French Romantic composer.

entries.clue: Delectable years on corporation, though not at first (5)

indicators.note: in a down clue, Y sits on top of what follows
TUMMY loses its first letter

blocks.note: a corporation is a paunch, a TUMMY, minus the T

annotation.surface: A company that has aged deliciously well, if not from the start.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Corporation' is dated British slang for a pot belly, which is the key to reading it as TUMMY rather than a company.
annotation.definitionFit: Yummy is the informal word for delicious, delectable.

entries.clue: Checks, excluding following 29 (5)

indicators.note: REBUFFS leaves out the FF

blocks.note: to rebuff = to check or repulse

annotation.walkthrough: 'ff.' is the abbreviation for 'following pages' in references, so FF comes out of REBUFFS.
annotation.definitionFit: A rebus is a picture puzzle standing for words, a kind of teaser.

entries.clue: Fake booze tucked into by sister, 29 (9)

indicators.note: NUN tucks into CODRUM, going inside it

blocks.note: cod = sham, mock, as in 'cod philosophy'
a sister is a nun, inserted after CO

annotation.surface: A nun caught helping herself to counterfeit rum.
annotation.walkthrough: CON for 'fake' is the tempting start, but it leaves the letters wrong; the fake is COD, a British adjective for mock or pretend.
annotation.definitionFit: A conundrum is a riddle or puzzling question, a teaser.

entries.clue: Not in favour of retaining form of light artistic tool (6)

indicators.note: CON keeps RAY held inside it

blocks.note: con = against, as in pros and cons
a ray is a form of light, placed inside

annotation.surface: An artist who dislikes a certain kind of lighting.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Of' looks like it glues 'light' to 'artistic tool', but it is only a link.
annotation.definitionFit: A crayon is a stick of coloured wax used for drawing.

entries.clue: Article in wrought iron, exotic source of abrasion (11)

indicators.note: A goes in among the other letters
wrought iron is worked, beaten into a new shape

annotation.surface: A foreign piece of ornamental ironwork, rough enough to graze the skin.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wrought iron' reads as a single phrase, but 'wrought' is the anagram signal and 'exotic' is fodder, not description.
annotation.definitionFit: Excoriation is the scraping away of skin, the action that causes an abrasion.

entries.clue: I initially considered you hostile (3)

indicators.note: take each word's initial letter

blocks.note: first letters of I, Considered, You

annotation.surface: Someone admitting their first impression was that you were unfriendly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Initially' sits after the first word but governs all three before 'hostile'.
annotation.definitionFit: Icy is used figuratively of manner: a cold, unwelcoming stare or greeting is hostile.

entries.clue: 29 quite soon sorted out, skipping an over (8)

indicators.note: the letters are sorted into a new order
one O is skipped over and left out

blocks.note: O = over in cricket scoring, removed

annotation.surface: A cricket report: the matter was settled quickly once an over was dropped.
annotation.walkthrough: An over is a set of six balls in cricket, abbreviated O on scorecards.
annotation.definitionFit: A question can be a puzzle to be answered, a teaser.

entries.clue: Arizona city: comments about person who is late here? (9)

annotation.definition2: comments about person who is late here?

blocks.note: the Wild West town of the OK Corral

blocks.clueFragment: comments about person who is late here?
blocks.note: a gravestone carries remarks about the deceased lying below

annotation.surface: A tourist sign in an Arizona town, grumbling about latecomers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Late' means dead, not tardy: a tombstone bears an epitaph about the person buried here.
annotation.definitionFit: Tombstone, Arizona, is the town of the gunfight at the OK Corral.

entries.clue: 29 turned up: last characters? The French (6)

indicators.note: something turned faces the other way, so UP is read backwards as PU

blocks.note: Z is the last letter of the alphabet, twice for the plural

annotation.walkthrough: 'Last characters' is not the end of some word: Z is the last character of the alphabet, and the plural asks for two.
annotation.definitionFit: A puzzle is a teaser, something that baffles.

entries.clue: Feature of a big mall, perhaps, or a castle, possibly (9)

annotation.definition: Feature of a big mall, perhaps

indicators.note: a possible rearrangement of the letters

annotation.surface: Wondering whether a great building is a shopping centre or a fortress.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Or' looks like it separates two definitions, but it is part of the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Escalators carry shoppers between floors in a large shopping mall.

entries.clue: Servant on the spot, turning up during supper? (6)

indicators.note: in a down clue, IN read upwards is NI
what happens during supper happens in the middle of it, so NI sits inside MEAL

annotation.surface: A servant who hovers at hand and pops up during dinner.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a butler at supper, which fits the answer neatly.
annotation.definitionFit: A menial is a domestic servant doing lowly work.

entries.clue: 29 moves in game (6)

indicators.note: letters that move shift out of their given places into a new order

annotation.walkthrough: 'Moves in game' reads as chess play; 'in' is fodder, not a container signal.
annotation.definitionFit: An enigma is a mystery or riddle, a teaser.

entries.clue: Blasphemy? I’m a matter for regret around Close in Carlisle (7)

indicators.note: PITY is placed around the E, one word wrapped round the other letter
the close of CARLISLE is its last letter

blocks.note: a pity = a matter for regret
last letter of CARLISLE, set inside PITY

annotation.definitionNote: Blasphemy is one example of impiety, hence the question mark.
annotation.surface: A confession of sacrilege in the precincts of Carlisle Cathedral.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Close' suggests a cathedral close, the grounds round a cathedral such as Carlisle's; here it means the end of the word.
annotation.definitionFit: Impiety is lack of reverence for God, of which blasphemy is an example.

entries.clue: Group in charge penning a line regarding display of shields (8)

indicators.note: HERD pens A and L inside, like animals in a fold

blocks.note: A plus L for line, penned inside HERD

annotation.surface: A committee in charge of a parade of shields writes a line about it.
annotation.walkthrough: IC is the abbreviation i/c for 'in charge'; although 'in charge' comes first in the clue, it goes at the end.
annotation.definitionFit: Heraldic means relating to heraldry, the design and display of coats of arms on shields.

entries.clue: Underhand opening for Dean and Prior to dismiss Priest (7)

indicators.note: the opening of DEAN is its first letter
to dismiss someone is to send them away, so PR is sent out of PREVIOUS

annotation.surface: Church politics: a dean and a prior plotting to sack a priest.
annotation.walkthrough: Dean, Prior and Priest all read as clergy; only Dean gives a letter, while Prior is the adjective PREVIOUS.
annotation.definitionFit: Devious literally means off the straight road, and figuratively scheming or underhand in dealings.

entries.clue: 29 days? Upset about that (6)

indicators.note: about in the sense of surrounding: RILE is placed about the days, enclosing them

blocks.note: D = day, twice for the plural, inside RILE

annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads 'days? Upset about that', so 'that' points back to the days: RILE goes around them.
annotation.definitionFit: A riddle is a puzzling question, a teaser.

entries.clue: University publisher and college at university (1,1,1)

blocks.note: to be up is to be in residence at university

annotation.surface: A university press and a college sharing a campus.
annotation.walkthrough: CUP is Cambridge University Press. Being 'up' at university is a British usage, especially for Oxford and Cambridge.
annotation.definitionFit: CUP stands for Cambridge University Press, a university publisher.

entries.clue: Chromium remains in accident (5)

blocks.note: ash is what remains after burning

annotation.surface: Chrome trim left among the wreckage of a car smash.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container signal, but it only links wordplay to definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Crash is the everyday word for a road or air accident involving a collision.

entries.clue: Gin or rum? Be frank: this is scarcely bubbly at all (6,5)

annotation.definition: this is scarcely bubbly at all

blocks.note: to level with someone is to be frank

annotation.surface: A drinker debating gin or rum, told straight that the choice is flat.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition plays on champagne: a spirit level holds just one bubble, so it is barely bubbly, unlike the drinks the surface suggests.
annotation.definitionFit: A spirit level is a builder's tool with a single air bubble in a liquid-filled tube.

entries.clue: Money: enticement to set about crossword at the outset (5)

indicators.note: set about means placed around, so LURE is put round the C
the outset of CROSSWORD is its first letter

blocks.note: first letter of CROSSWORD, set inside LURE

annotation.surface: A cash prize dangled to get people started on a crossword.
annotation.walkthrough: Lucre, as in 'filthy lucre', is an old word for money, usually disapproving.
annotation.definitionFit: Lucre is money, especially when gained dishonourably.

entries.clue: Broadcast i.e. a Donald, with an affected voice? (9)

indicators.note: broadcast seed is scattered, so the letters are thrown about

annotation.surface: A radio broadcast by someone called Donald, in an odd put-on voice.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that an adenoidal voice is nasal from swollen adenoids, 'affected' in the medical sense rather than put on.
annotation.definitionFit: An adenoidal voice sounds nasal and blocked, as if the adenoids were enlarged.

entries.clue: Chlorine not to be used? That’s a blow (5)

blocks.note: out = unavailable, not to be used

annotation.surface: Pool staff announce no chlorine today, a real setback.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not to be used' suggests removing letters, but it is simply OUT, as when a road or a player is out.
annotation.definitionFit: Clout is an informal British word for a hard hit, especially with the hand; it also means influence.

entries.clue: Seasonal problem play by Coward (3,5)

annotation.surface: A critic grumbles about a Coward play being staged every summer.
annotation.walkthrough: Noël Coward was an English playwright; 'Hay Fever' is among his best-known comedies.
annotation.definitionFit: Hay fever is an allergy to pollen that strikes in spring and summer.

entries.clue: Anagram, perhaps, seen in Easter? (6)

indicators.note: the clue names the device outright

annotation.surface: A word puzzle printed in a holiday special.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: a teaser such as an anagram, and TEASER is itself an anagram of EASTER. This is the answer the other 29 clues refer to.
annotation.definitionFit: A teaser is a tricky puzzle, and an anagram is one kind.
